### 3.3. (−)-Carveol biosynthesis from (−)-limonene
(−)-Carveol is a naturally oxygenated derivative of limonene, catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 enzyme (L6H) [ 44 , 45 ]. In addition, the L6H requires a cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR) to maintain its proper catalysis activity [ 46 ]. To convert (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, we recruited the Mentha x gracilis originated L6H ( Mg L6H) and the CPR from Arabidopsis thaliana ( At CPR) by putting them under the native pLDP1 ( Fig. 4 ), which have been demonstrated efficiency for limonene derivatives. Considering that the plant-derived P450s exhibit significant challenges for heterologous expression, including low catalytic efficiency and frequent substrate promiscuity [ 47 ], we strategically avoided using the strain SL12 with the highest (−)-limonene titer as the chassis cell. Instead, the medium strain SL4 that produced 51.0 mg/L (−)-limonene was chosen to circumvent excessive precursor accumulation.
Engineering the (−)-carveol biosynthesis. (A) The retention of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol on the gas chromatogram. The (−)-carveol standard mixtures were composed of (−)-cis-carveol and (−)-trans-carveol with a ratio of 11: 9. (B) The mass spectrum of (−)-carveol standard and the sample. (C) and (D) Optimization of the (−)-carveol synthesis by reinforcement the expression of critical genes in catalyzing carveol production and the MVA pathway. ns, no significant difference, ∗, p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗, p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.001; ∗∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.0001 (two-tailed unpaired Student's t -test). The experiments were conducted in triplicate and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. As expected, when the Mg L6H and At CPR were co-integrated into the genome of SL4, the resultant strain SC1 produced 22.9 mg/L (−)-carveol at an 80.6% ratio, with 5.2 mg/L (−)-limonene left ( Fig. 4 C) in NL medium at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The accumulation of (−)-limonene indicated that the (−)-carveol synthesis enzyme activity was less efficient and required further optimizati

### 3.4. Engineering the (−)-carvone biosynthesis
(−)-Carvone is converted from (−)-carveol via the carveol dehydrogenase (CDH) [ 50 ]. To construct the whole (−)-carvone biosynthesis pathway, six CDHs from distinct sources were evaluated with the (−)-carveol producing strain SC9. Phylogenetic analysis revealed evolutionary divergence among these enzymes, which might help the finding of CDH with desired activity ( Fig. S2B ). The (−)-carvone production suggested that the most efficient one was from R. erythropolis ( Re CDH) , which generated 5 mg/L (−)-carvone in 50-mL test tube ( Fig. 5 B). However, there were still a lot of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol left, which might be attributed to the undesired enzymatic activity ( Fig. 5 C). We thus hypothesized that the common metabolic engineering practice, increasing the gene copy numbers of the critical CDH would enhance the (−)-carvone production. As expected, the (−)-carvone was improved to 30 mg/L when the four copies of CDH were introduced into R. toruloides ( Fig. 5 D). While a sharp reduction in (−)-carveol accumulation was observed, a comparable amount of (−)-limonene was still produced ( Fig. 5 D). Moreover, our results also showed that the composition of the monoterpenoids were also strain-dependent as the sub-clones of the strain SE4 affected different monoterpenoids spectra ( Fig. 5 E). Furthermore, the (–)-carveol contents varied among tested subclones while the residue limonene remained almost comparable, suggesting that the conversion efficiency of limonene to carveol should be given more consideration. To ensure the satisfactory production of (−)-carvone, highly efficient L6H and CDH should be further explored.

### 3.5. Increase monoterpenoids production by fed-batch fermentation
We further increased (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production by fed-batch fermentation using SL14, SC9 and SE4, respectively. Prior to fed-batch fermentation, the influence of C/N ratios (15:1, 30:1, 60:1, 120:1, and 240:1) on (−)-limonene production was evaluated in 250-mL shake flask using SL9 since the availability of nutrients critically influences microbial growth and metabolic activity ( Fig. S3 ). Comparable (−)-limonene production was obtained when the C/N ratios were 15:1, 30:1 and 60:1 while severe impaired cell growth was observed with the C/N ratios of 120:1 and 240:1. The fed-batch fermentation results on 500-mL bioreactors demonstrated that the C/N ratio of 15:1 outperformed 30:1 and 60:1 since the highest (−)-limonene titer of 608.5 mg/L was achieved with a C/N ratio of 15:1 at 156 h ( Fig. S4 ). Subsequently, we scaled up the fermentation system to a 3-L bioreactor with a C/N ratio of 15:1 ( Fig. 6 A), which commenced the (−)-limonene production at 48 h, and maximized with a final production of 1.6 g/L and 19.0 mg/g glucose at 144 h.
Fed-batch fermentation of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol. (A) SL14 for (−)-limonene production and (B) SC9 for (−)-carveol production in 3-L bioreactors. The experiments were conducted in triplicate, and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. The C/N ratio of 15:1 was also applied to conduct the fed-batch fermentation of (−)-carveol with strain SC9 in the 3-L bioreactor, where the final (−)-carveol titer reached 668.0 mg/L at 240 h. However, a very high residue of (−)-limonene (361.7 mg/L) was also observed, 36% of the total monoterpenoids production ( Fig. 6 B). The significant accumulation of limonene suggested the hydroxylation of (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, determined by L6H and CPR, was a bottleneck for efficient (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production. The apparent increase in (−)-limonene accumulation in the bioreactors indicated the L6H catalytic efficiency was severely compromised,

De novo production of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone via engineering Rhodotorula toruloides

### Abstract
De novo biosynthesis of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone was achieved via rewiring the mevalonate pathway in the oleaginous yeast Rhodotorula toruloides . Strategies including enzyme selection, protein fusion, pathway optimization (MVA upstream enhancement, cofactor supply), and fermentation condition optimization were applied to improve the monoterpenoids production. Finally, the (−)-limonene titer of 1.6 g/L and (−)-carveol of 668.0 mg/L were achieved through fed-batch fermentation in a 3-L bioreactor. Furthermore, the feasibility of biosynthesis of (−)-carvone was also demonstrated. This study represents an example for de novo microbial production of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone with the oleaginous red yeast R. toruloides , demonstrating its potential as a versatile chassis for monoterpenoid biosynthesis.

### 1. Introduction
Isoprene-derived monoterpenes find broad applications in food, pharmaceuticals, fragrances [ 1 , 2 ]. Among all the monoterpenes, (+)-limonene and (−)-limonene are enantiomers that possess distinct aromatic attributes [ 3 ]. While (+)-limonene is directly used as flavors, solvents and industrial feedstocks, (−)-limonene serves as precursors for valuable oxygenated monoterpenoids, such as (−)-menthol and perillic acid, which exhibits more desirable fragrance properties, significant economic and pharmacological values [ [4] , [5] , [6] ].
The traditional production of limonene and its oxygenated derivatives from plant sources usually faces uncertainties caused by climate variability, environmental changes, and cultivation area constraints. Additionally, chemical-based synthesis route suffers from compromised product selectivity, environmental pollution, and toxic impurities [ 7 ]. The rapid advance in synthetic biology and metabolic engineering offers an alternative strategy for the sustainable synthesis of high-value natural products [ 8 ]. Microbial production of limonene and its derivatives, such as perillyl alcohol, perillic acid and (+)-carveol, have been documented in Escherichia coli [ 9 ], Candida tropicalis [ 6 ], Saccharomyces cerevisiae [ 1 , 10 ], Yarrowia lipolytica [ 11 ], and Rhodotorula toruloides [ 7 ]. However, the de novo microbial production of (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone has been rarely reported ( Table 1 , Table 2 , Table 3 ).

Open in a new tab For facilitating monoterpenoids microbial production, the commonly employed strategies include: (i) screening natural enzymes with desired efficiency [ 6 , 17 ]; (ii) engineering enzymes through rational design or directed evolution [ 18 ]; (iii) fusing sequential and determinant enzymes to avoid metabolite flux leakage and accelerate substrate transformation [ 19 ]; (iv) optimizing the key knots in the biosynthesis pathway while down-tuning the competitive route to streamline precursor and intermediates supply toward downstream conversion [ 6 ]; (v) engineering the redox balance by recycling the essential cofactors like NAD(P)H [ 8 ]. Besides the integrated use of the metabolic engineering approaches, an appropriate microbial host can also contribute to the establishment of a monoterpenoid cell factory.
Although it currently has a less advanced genetic editing toolbox, the red yeast Rhodotorula toruloides is exhibiting attractive properties as a promising microbial cell factory for terpenoid production with the fast development of synthetic biology and metabolic engineering technology. Importantly, it harbors rich pool of acetyl-CoA and NADPH, broad substrate spectrum and outstanding high-density fermentation capacity. Besides, it has stronger robustness than other oleaginous yeasts such as Y. lipolytica in harsh conditions, which offers the advantage of refining low-cost feedstocks, such as non-detoxified hydrolysates of agricultural lignocellulosic biomass, toward value-added products [ [20] , [21] , [22] ]. Notably, it exhibits high tolerance to up to 2.0 g/L limonene, making it promising for limonene and derivatives production [ 22 ]. Additionally, it has been successfully engineered to produce a wide range of valuable compounds such as linalool, lipids and carotenoids [ [23] , [24] , [25] ]. Taken together, the natural attributes mentioned above position R. toruloides as a highly interesting chassis fo

### 2.1. Strains and culture conditions
Plasmid construction and propagation were conducted with E. coli DH5α in Luria−Bertani (LB) medium, supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin at 37 °C. LB medium was also used for cultivation of Agrobacterium tumefaciens AGL1 at 28 °C. The haploid R. toruloides NP11 was donated by Prof. Zongbao Zhao. If not specified, the yeast strains were cultured in nitrogen-limiting (NL) medium that were kept at 22 °C and 180 rpm for a time range as needed. Antibiotics (G418, nourseothricin, or zeocin, 50 μg/mL) were used for identifying yeast transformants in both liquid and solid YPD media (20 g/L agar was added into liquid YPD).

### 2.2. Plasmid construction
The vector pZPK was employed to construct all the necessary expression cassettes in this study [ 27 ]. The plasmids and primers used in this study are provided in supplementary materials. The DNA Ligation Kit Ver.2.1 (Takara) and In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara) were employed for constructing the vectors. All the genes used in this study were optimized according to the codon bias of R. toruloides and synthesized by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, P. R. China). The codon usage of the heterologous genes was redressed according to the preference of R. toruloides and produced by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, China). The heterologous (−)-LS genes were Cs tLS from Cannabis sativa ( NP_001384867.1 ), Et tLS from Eleutherococcus trifoliatus ( AIO10970.1 ), Ml tLS from Mentha longifolia ( WAB06559.1 ), Ms tLS from Mentha spicata ( QBA83293.1 ), Pa tLS from Pinus armandii Franch ( UNY86182.1 ), and Ps tLS from Picea abies ( AAS47694.1 ). The carvone dehydrogenase genes were Ab CDH from Actinobacteria bacterium (MGW3291715.1), Mp CDH from Mentha × piperita ( QPI35669.1 ), Re CDH from Rhodococcus erythropolis ( WP_076949156.1 ), Sh CDH from Streptomyces himastatinicus ( WP_009719709.1 ), Mt CDH from Mycolicibacterium thermoresistibile ( WP_448509721.1 ) and M y s CDH from Mycobacterium sp (HYJ57287.1). The acetoacetyl-CoA synthase NphT7, ( D7URV0 .1), Acetyl-CoA acetyl-transferase/HMGR ( Ef MvaE, AF290092 ), HMG-CoA synthase ( Ef MvaS, AF290092 ), Mevalonate kinase ( Mm MK, AAM31458 ). The native ATP-citrate lyase (ACL, RHTO_03915) was cloned from the cDNA of R . toruloides NP11. 2.3. Construction of recombinant R. toruloides

### 2.4. Fermentation of engineered strains
For flask fermentation, colonies were pre-cultured in 50-mL test tubes, containing 5 mL of YPD medium, at 28 °C, 180 rpm until OD 600 reached 10–12. Then, they were inoculated at an initial OD 600 of 0.5 in the 250-mL shake flasks (containing 50 mL NL, YPD or MM medium) and cultivated at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The carbon source used for production was 20 g/L glucose. Isopropyl myristate (IPM) was used as an overlay 20% (v/v) for the instant extraction of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone.

### 3.1. Construction of the (−)-limonene biosynthesis baseline
Limonene can be synthesized through the MVA and/or MEP pathway with geranyl diphosphate (GPP) and/or NPP as the direct precursor [ 19 ]. The biosynthesis of limonene is controlled by several rate-limiting enzyme, such as HMGR, IDI, GPP and/or NPP synthase and limonene synthase (LS) [ 6 , 7 ]. Moreover, fermentation conditions influence the cell viability and the final chemical productivity. Particularly, the carbon flux will be mostly directed towards lipid biosynthesis in R . toruloides under nutrient depleted conditions, such as nitrogen limitation [ 30 ]. Fortunately, we have previously constructed a MVA, NPP and fusion protein based limonene biosynthesis route, developed a mutant FPPS from R. toruloides (FPPS F91W/N122W/K192G , hereafter denoted as FPPS∗∗∗) to boost the efficient linalool synthesis in R. toruloides and isolated a strong promoter pLDP in NL medium [ 22 ].
Considering that the catalytic efficiency of the (−)-limonene synthase ((−)-LS) is crucial for high-yield biosynthesis, we first employed the most reported (−)-LS from Mentha spicata ( Ms tLS) to construct the (−)-limonene synthesis pathway [ 8 , 10 ]. It was fused to the FPPS∗∗∗ (FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS) with the GGGS linker, the most commonly used strategy to enhance the precuror transfer and limonene production [ 8 ]. To ensure the precursor supply, the critical enzymes HMGR was linked with FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS by P2A peptide and overexpressed simultaneously using the strong promoter pLDP1 ( Fig. 2 ). Then, five other distinct (−)-LSs (Phylogenetic analysis, Fig. S2A ) were fused to FPPS∗∗∗ with GGGS linker and compared for their capacity in supporting (−)-limonene production. The results showed that Ms tLS was the most effective among all the candidates ( Fig. 2 A). To further verify our results, we investigated the limonene production with the fusion protein ( Ms tLS-FPPS∗∗∗), and separate expression of Ms tLS and FPPS∗∗∗ mediated by P2A peptide. We also managed to constructed the nerol pyrophosphate (N

### 3.2. Strengthening the upper pathway and NADPH supply leads to enhanced (−)-limonene production
Optimizing the design of metabolic pathways is paramount for achieving efficient microbial synthesis of desired products. The MVA-based limonene synthesis pathway is initiated with the acetoacetyl-CoA, which is produced from condensing acetyl-CoA by gate-keeper enzyme ACCT, or acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA by the acac-CoA synthase (NphT7) from Streptomyces sp. ( Fig. 1 , Fig. 3 A) [ 31 , 32 ].

### 3.3. (−)-Carveol biosynthesis from (−)-limonene
(−)-Carveol is a naturally oxygenated derivative of limonene, catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 enzyme (L6H) [ 44 , 45 ]. In addition, the L6H requires a cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR) to maintain its proper catalysis activity [ 46 ]. To convert (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, we recruited the Mentha x gracilis originated L6H ( Mg L6H) and the CPR from Arabidopsis thaliana ( At CPR) by putting them under the native pLDP1 ( Fig. 4 ), which have been demonstrated efficiency for limonene derivatives. Considering that the plant-derived P450s exhibit significant challenges for heterologous expression, including low catalytic efficiency and frequent substrate promiscuity [ 47 ], we strategically avoided using the strain SL12 with the highest (−)-limonene titer as the chassis cell. Instead, the medium strain SL4 that produced 51.0 mg/L (−)-limonene was chosen to circumvent excessive precursor accumulation.
Engineering the (−)-carveol biosynthesis. (A) The retention of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol on the gas chromatogram. The (−)-carveol standard mixtures were composed of (−)-cis-carveol and (−)-trans-carveol with a ratio of 11: 9. (B) The mass spectrum of (−)-carveol standard and the sample. (C) and (D) Optimization of the (−)-carveol synthesis by reinforcement the expression of critical genes in catalyzing carveol production and the MVA pathway. ns, no significant difference, ∗, p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗, p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.001; ∗∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.0001 (two-tailed unpaired Student's t -test). The experiments were conducted in triplicate and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. As expected, when the Mg L6H and At CPR were co-integrated into the genome of SL4, the resultant strain SC1 produced 22.9 mg/L (−)-carveol at an 80.6% ratio, with 5.2 mg/L (−)-limonene left ( Fig. 4 C) in NL medium at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The accumulation of (−)-limonene indicated that the (−)-carveol synthesis enzyme activity was less efficient and required further optimizati

### 3.4. Engineering the (−)-carvone biosynthesis
(−)-Carvone is converted from (−)-carveol via the carveol dehydrogenase (CDH) [ 50 ]. To construct the whole (−)-carvone biosynthesis pathway, six CDHs from distinct sources were evaluated with the (−)-carveol producing strain SC9. Phylogenetic analysis revealed evolutionary divergence among these enzymes, which might help the finding of CDH with desired activity ( Fig. S2B ). The (−)-carvone production suggested that the most efficient one was from R. erythropolis ( Re CDH) , which generated 5 mg/L (−)-carvone in 50-mL test tube ( Fig. 5 B). However, there were still a lot of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol left, which might be attributed to the undesired enzymatic activity ( Fig. 5 C). We thus hypothesized that the common metabolic engineering practice, increasing the gene copy numbers of the critical CDH would enhance the (−)-carvone production. As expected, the (−)-carvone was improved to 30 mg/L when the four copies of CDH were introduced into R. toruloides ( Fig. 5 D). While a sharp reduction in (−)-carveol accumulation was observed, a comparable amount of (−)-limonene was still produced ( Fig. 5 D). Moreover, our results also showed that the composition of the monoterpenoids were also strain-dependent as the sub-clones of the strain SE4 affected different monoterpenoids spectra ( Fig. 5 E). Furthermore, the (–)-carveol contents varied among tested subclones while the residue limonene remained almost comparable, suggesting that the conversion efficiency of limonene to carveol should be given more consideration. To ensure the satisfactory production of (−)-carvone, highly efficient L6H and CDH should be further explored.

### 3.5. Increase monoterpenoids production by fed-batch fermentation
We further increased (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production by fed-batch fermentation using SL14, SC9 and SE4, respectively. Prior to fed-batch fermentation, the influence of C/N ratios (15:1, 30:1, 60:1, 120:1, and 240:1) on (−)-limonene production was evaluated in 250-mL shake flask using SL9 since the availability of nutrients critically influences microbial growth and metabolic activity ( Fig. S3 ). Comparable (−)-limonene production was obtained when the C/N ratios were 15:1, 30:1 and 60:1 while severe impaired cell growth was observed with the C/N ratios of 120:1 and 240:1. The fed-batch fermentation results on 500-mL bioreactors demonstrated that the C/N ratio of 15:1 outperformed 30:1 and 60:1 since the highest (−)-limonene titer of 608.5 mg/L was achieved with a C/N ratio of 15:1 at 156 h ( Fig. S4 ). Subsequently, we scaled up the fermentation system to a 3-L bioreactor with a C/N ratio of 15:1 ( Fig. 6 A), which commenced the (−)-limonene production at 48 h, and maximized with a final production of 1.6 g/L and 19.0 mg/g glucose at 144 h.
Fed-batch fermentation of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol. (A) SL14 for (−)-limonene production and (B) SC9 for (−)-carveol production in 3-L bioreactors. The experiments were conducted in triplicate, and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. The C/N ratio of 15:1 was also applied to conduct the fed-batch fermentation of (−)-carveol with strain SC9 in the 3-L bioreactor, where the final (−)-carveol titer reached 668.0 mg/L at 240 h. However, a very high residue of (−)-limonene (361.7 mg/L) was also observed, 36% of the total monoterpenoids production ( Fig. 6 B). The significant accumulation of limonene suggested the hydroxylation of (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, determined by L6H and CPR, was a bottleneck for efficient (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production. The apparent increase in (−)-limonene accumulation in the bioreactors indicated the L6H catalytic efficiency was severely compromised,

### Abstract
De novo biosynthesis of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone was achieved via rewiring the mevalonate pathway in the oleaginous yeast Rhodotorula toruloides . Strategies including enzyme selection, protein fusion, pathway optimization (MVA upstream enhancement, cofactor supply), and fermentation condition optimization were applied to improve the monoterpenoids production. Finally, the (−)-limonene titer of 1.6 g/L and (−)-carveol of 668.0 mg/L were achieved through fed-batch fermentation in a 3-L bioreactor. Furthermore, the feasibility of biosynthesis of (−)-carvone was also demonstrated. This study represents an example for de novo microbial production of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone with the oleaginous red yeast R. toruloides , demonstrating its potential as a versatile chassis for monoterpenoid biosynthesis.

### 1. Introduction
Isoprene-derived monoterpenes find broad applications in food, pharmaceuticals, fragrances [ 1 , 2 ]. Among all the monoterpenes, (+)-limonene and (−)-limonene are enantiomers that possess distinct aromatic attributes [ 3 ]. While (+)-limonene is directly used as flavors, solvents and industrial feedstocks, (−)-limonene serves as precursors for valuable oxygenated monoterpenoids, such as (−)-menthol and perillic acid, which exhibits more desirable fragrance properties, significant economic and pharmacological values [ [4] , [5] , [6] ].
The traditional production of limonene and its oxygenated derivatives from plant sources usually faces uncertainties caused by climate variability, environmental changes, and cultivation area constraints. Additionally, chemical-based synthesis route suffers from compromised product selectivity, environmental pollution, and toxic impurities [ 7 ]. The rapid advance in synthetic biology and metabolic engineering offers an alternative strategy for the sustainable synthesis of high-value natural products [ 8 ]. Microbial production of limonene and its derivatives, such as perillyl alcohol, perillic acid and (+)-carveol, have been documented in Escherichia coli [ 9 ], Candida tropicalis [ 6 ], Saccharomyces cerevisiae [ 1 , 10 ], Yarrowia lipolytica [ 11 ], and Rhodotorula toruloides [ 7 ]. However, the de novo microbial production of (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone has been rarely reported ( Table 1 , Table 2 , Table 3 ).

Open in a new tab For facilitating monoterpenoids microbial production, the commonly employed strategies include: (i) screening natural enzymes with desired efficiency [ 6 , 17 ]; (ii) engineering enzymes through rational design or directed evolution [ 18 ]; (iii) fusing sequential and determinant enzymes to avoid metabolite flux leakage and accelerate substrate transformation [ 19 ]; (iv) optimizing the key knots in the biosynthesis pathway while down-tuning the competitive route to streamline precursor and intermediates supply toward downstream conversion [ 6 ]; (v) engineering the redox balance by recycling the essential cofactors like NAD(P)H [ 8 ]. Besides the integrated use of the metabolic engineering approaches, an appropriate microbial host can also contribute to the establishment of a monoterpenoid cell factory.
Although it currently has a less advanced genetic editing toolbox, the red yeast Rhodotorula toruloides is exhibiting attractive properties as a promising microbial cell factory for terpenoid production with the fast development of synthetic biology and metabolic engineering technology. Importantly, it harbors rich pool of acetyl-CoA and NADPH, broad substrate spectrum and outstanding high-density fermentation capacity. Besides, it has stronger robustness than other oleaginous yeasts such as Y. lipolytica in harsh conditions, which offers the advantage of refining low-cost feedstocks, such as non-detoxified hydrolysates of agricultural lignocellulosic biomass, toward value-added products [ [20] , [21] , [22] ]. Notably, it exhibits high tolerance to up to 2.0 g/L limonene, making it promising for limonene and derivatives production [ 22 ]. Additionally, it has been successfully engineered to produce a wide range of valuable compounds such as linalool, lipids and carotenoids [ [23] , [24] , [25] ]. Taken together, the natural attributes mentioned above position R. toruloides as a highly interesting chassis fo

### 2.1. Strains and culture conditions
Plasmid construction and propagation were conducted with E. coli DH5α in Luria−Bertani (LB) medium, supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin at 37 °C. LB medium was also used for cultivation of Agrobacterium tumefaciens AGL1 at 28 °C. The haploid R. toruloides NP11 was donated by Prof. Zongbao Zhao. If not specified, the yeast strains were cultured in nitrogen-limiting (NL) medium that were kept at 22 °C and 180 rpm for a time range as needed. Antibiotics (G418, nourseothricin, or zeocin, 50 μg/mL) were used for identifying yeast transformants in both liquid and solid YPD media (20 g/L agar was added into liquid YPD).

### 2.2. Plasmid construction
The vector pZPK was employed to construct all the necessary expression cassettes in this study [ 27 ]. The plasmids and primers used in this study are provided in supplementary materials. The DNA Ligation Kit Ver.2.1 (Takara) and In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara) were employed for constructing the vectors. All the genes used in this study were optimized according to the codon bias of R. toruloides and synthesized by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, P. R. China). The codon usage of the heterologous genes was redressed according to the preference of R. toruloides and produced by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, China). The heterologous (−)-LS genes were Cs tLS from Cannabis sativa ( NP_001384867.1 ), Et tLS from Eleutherococcus trifoliatus ( AIO10970.1 ), Ml tLS from Mentha longifolia ( WAB06559.1 ), Ms tLS from Mentha spicata ( QBA83293.1 ), Pa tLS from Pinus armandii Franch ( UNY86182.1 ), and Ps tLS from Picea abies ( AAS47694.1 ). The carvone dehydrogenase genes were Ab CDH from Actinobacteria bacterium (MGW3291715.1), Mp CDH from Mentha × piperita ( QPI35669.1 ), Re CDH from Rhodococcus erythropolis ( WP_076949156.1 ), Sh CDH from Streptomyces himastatinicus ( WP_009719709.1 ), Mt CDH from Mycolicibacterium thermoresistibile ( WP_448509721.1 ) and M y s CDH from Mycobacterium sp (HYJ57287.1). The acetoacetyl-CoA synthase NphT7, ( D7URV0 .1), Acetyl-CoA acetyl-transferase/HMGR ( Ef MvaE, AF290092 ), HMG-CoA synthase ( Ef MvaS, AF290092 ), Mevalonate kinase ( Mm MK, AAM31458 ). The native ATP-citrate lyase (ACL, RHTO_03915) was cloned from the cDNA of R . toruloides NP11. 2.3. Construction of recombinant R. toruloides

### 2.4. Fermentation of engineered strains
For flask fermentation, colonies were pre-cultured in 50-mL test tubes, containing 5 mL of YPD medium, at 28 °C, 180 rpm until OD 600 reached 10–12. Then, they were inoculated at an initial OD 600 of 0.5 in the 250-mL shake flasks (containing 50 mL NL, YPD or MM medium) and cultivated at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The carbon source used for production was 20 g/L glucose. Isopropyl myristate (IPM) was used as an overlay 20% (v/v) for the instant extraction of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone.

### 3.1. Construction of the (−)-limonene biosynthesis baseline
Limonene can be synthesized through the MVA and/or MEP pathway with geranyl diphosphate (GPP) and/or NPP as the direct precursor [ 19 ]. The biosynthesis of limonene is controlled by several rate-limiting enzyme, such as HMGR, IDI, GPP and/or NPP synthase and limonene synthase (LS) [ 6 , 7 ]. Moreover, fermentation conditions influence the cell viability and the final chemical productivity. Particularly, the carbon flux will be mostly directed towards lipid biosynthesis in R . toruloides under nutrient depleted conditions, such as nitrogen limitation [ 30 ]. Fortunately, we have previously constructed a MVA, NPP and fusion protein based limonene biosynthesis route, developed a mutant FPPS from R. toruloides (FPPS F91W/N122W/K192G , hereafter denoted as FPPS∗∗∗) to boost the efficient linalool synthesis in R. toruloides and isolated a strong promoter pLDP in NL medium [ 22 ].
Considering that the catalytic efficiency of the (−)-limonene synthase ((−)-LS) is crucial for high-yield biosynthesis, we first employed the most reported (−)-LS from Mentha spicata ( Ms tLS) to construct the (−)-limonene synthesis pathway [ 8 , 10 ]. It was fused to the FPPS∗∗∗ (FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS) with the GGGS linker, the most commonly used strategy to enhance the precuror transfer and limonene production [ 8 ]. To ensure the precursor supply, the critical enzymes HMGR was linked with FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS by P2A peptide and overexpressed simultaneously using the strong promoter pLDP1 ( Fig. 2 ). Then, five other distinct (−)-LSs (Phylogenetic analysis, Fig. S2A ) were fused to FPPS∗∗∗ with GGGS linker and compared for their capacity in supporting (−)-limonene production. The results showed that Ms tLS was the most effective among all the candidates ( Fig. 2 A). To further verify our results, we investigated the limonene production with the fusion protein ( Ms tLS-FPPS∗∗∗), and separate expression of Ms tLS and FPPS∗∗∗ mediated by P2A peptide. We also managed to constructed the nerol pyrophosphate (N

### 3.2. Strengthening the upper pathway and NADPH supply leads to enhanced (−)-limonene production
Optimizing the design of metabolic pathways is paramount for achieving efficient microbial synthesis of desired products. The MVA-based limonene synthesis pathway is initiated with the acetoacetyl-CoA, which is produced from condensing acetyl-CoA by gate-keeper enzyme ACCT, or acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA by the acac-CoA synthase (NphT7) from Streptomyces sp. ( Fig. 1 , Fig. 3 A) [ 31 , 32 ].

### 3.3. (−)-Carveol biosynthesis from (−)-limonene
(−)-Carveol is a naturally oxygenated derivative of limonene, catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 enzyme (L6H) [ 44 , 45 ]. In addition, the L6H requires a cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR) to maintain its proper catalysis activity [ 46 ]. To convert (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, we recruited the Mentha x gracilis originated L6H ( Mg L6H) and the CPR from Arabidopsis thaliana ( At CPR) by putting them under the native pLDP1 ( Fig. 4 ), which have been demonstrated efficiency for limonene derivatives. Considering that the plant-derived P450s exhibit significant challenges for heterologous expression, including low catalytic efficiency and frequent substrate promiscuity [ 47 ], we strategically avoided using the strain SL12 with the highest (−)-limonene titer as the chassis cell. Instead, the medium strain SL4 that produced 51.0 mg/L (−)-limonene was chosen to circumvent excessive precursor accumulation.
Engineering the (−)-carveol biosynthesis. (A) The retention of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol on the gas chromatogram. The (−)-carveol standard mixtures were composed of (−)-cis-carveol and (−)-trans-carveol with a ratio of 11: 9. (B) The mass spectrum of (−)-carveol standard and the sample. (C) and (D) Optimization of the (−)-carveol synthesis by reinforcement the expression of critical genes in catalyzing carveol production and the MVA pathway. ns, no significant difference, ∗, p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗, p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.001; ∗∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.0001 (two-tailed unpaired Student's t -test). The experiments were conducted in triplicate and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. As expected, when the Mg L6H and At CPR were co-integrated into the genome of SL4, the resultant strain SC1 produced 22.9 mg/L (−)-carveol at an 80.6% ratio, with 5.2 mg/L (−)-limonene left ( Fig. 4 C) in NL medium at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The accumulation of (−)-limonene indicated that the (−)-carveol synthesis enzyme activity was less efficient and required further optimizati

### 3.4. Engineering the (−)-carvone biosynthesis
(−)-Carvone is converted from (−)-carveol via the carveol dehydrogenase (CDH) [ 50 ]. To construct the whole (−)-carvone biosynthesis pathway, six CDHs from distinct sources were evaluated with the (−)-carveol producing strain SC9. Phylogenetic analysis revealed evolutionary divergence among these enzymes, which might help the finding of CDH with desired activity ( Fig. S2B ). The (−)-carvone production suggested that the most efficient one was from R. erythropolis ( Re CDH) , which generated 5 mg/L (−)-carvone in 50-mL test tube ( Fig. 5 B). However, there were still a lot of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol left, which might be attributed to the undesired enzymatic activity ( Fig. 5 C). We thus hypothesized that the common metabolic engineering practice, increasing the gene copy numbers of the critical CDH would enhance the (−)-carvone production. As expected, the (−)-carvone was improved to 30 mg/L when the four copies of CDH were introduced into R. toruloides ( Fig. 5 D). While a sharp reduction in (−)-carveol accumulation was observed, a comparable amount of (−)-limonene was still produced ( Fig. 5 D). Moreover, our results also showed that the composition of the monoterpenoids were also strain-dependent as the sub-clones of the strain SE4 affected different monoterpenoids spectra ( Fig. 5 E). Furthermore, the (–)-carveol contents varied among tested subclones while the residue limonene remained almost comparable, suggesting that the conversion efficiency of limonene to carveol should be given more consideration. To ensure the satisfactory production of (−)-carvone, highly efficient L6H and CDH should be further explored.

### 3.5. Increase monoterpenoids production by fed-batch fermentation
We further increased (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production by fed-batch fermentation using SL14, SC9 and SE4, respectively. Prior to fed-batch fermentation, the influence of C/N ratios (15:1, 30:1, 60:1, 120:1, and 240:1) on (−)-limonene production was evaluated in 250-mL shake flask using SL9 since the availability of nutrients critically influences microbial growth and metabolic activity ( Fig. S3 ). Comparable (−)-limonene production was obtained when the C/N ratios were 15:1, 30:1 and 60:1 while severe impaired cell growth was observed with the C/N ratios of 120:1 and 240:1. The fed-batch fermentation results on 500-mL bioreactors demonstrated that the C/N ratio of 15:1 outperformed 30:1 and 60:1 since the highest (−)-limonene titer of 608.5 mg/L was achieved with a C/N ratio of 15:1 at 156 h ( Fig. S4 ). Subsequently, we scaled up the fermentation system to a 3-L bioreactor with a C/N ratio of 15:1 ( Fig. 6 A), which commenced the (−)-limonene production at 48 h, and maximized with a final production of 1.6 g/L and 19.0 mg/g glucose at 144 h.
Fed-batch fermentation of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol. (A) SL14 for (−)-limonene production and (B) SC9 for (−)-carveol production in 3-L bioreactors. The experiments were conducted in triplicate, and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. The C/N ratio of 15:1 was also applied to conduct the fed-batch fermentation of (−)-carveol with strain SC9 in the 3-L bioreactor, where the final (−)-carveol titer reached 668.0 mg/L at 240 h. However, a very high residue of (−)-limonene (361.7 mg/L) was also observed, 36% of the total monoterpenoids production ( Fig. 6 B). The significant accumulation of limonene suggested the hydroxylation of (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, determined by L6H and CPR, was a bottleneck for efficient (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production. The apparent increase in (−)-limonene accumulation in the bioreactors indicated the L6H catalytic efficiency was severely compromised,

### Abstract
De novo biosynthesis of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone was achieved via rewiring the mevalonate pathway in the oleaginous yeast Rhodotorula toruloides . Strategies including enzyme selection, protein fusion, pathway optimization (MVA upstream enhancement, cofactor supply), and fermentation condition optimization were applied to improve the monoterpenoids production. Finally, the (−)-limonene titer of 1.6 g/L and (−)-carveol of 668.0 mg/L were achieved through fed-batch fermentation in a 3-L bioreactor. Furthermore, the feasibility of biosynthesis of (−)-carvone was also demonstrated. This study represents an example for de novo microbial production of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone with the oleaginous red yeast R. toruloides , demonstrating its potential as a versatile chassis for monoterpenoid biosynthesis.

### 1. Introduction
Isoprene-derived monoterpenes find broad applications in food, pharmaceuticals, fragrances [ 1 , 2 ]. Among all the monoterpenes, (+)-limonene and (−)-limonene are enantiomers that possess distinct aromatic attributes [ 3 ]. While (+)-limonene is directly used as flavors, solvents and industrial feedstocks, (−)-limonene serves as precursors for valuable oxygenated monoterpenoids, such as (−)-menthol and perillic acid, which exhibits more desirable fragrance properties, significant economic and pharmacological values [ [4] , [5] , [6] ].
The traditional production of limonene and its oxygenated derivatives from plant sources usually faces uncertainties caused by climate variability, environmental changes, and cultivation area constraints. Additionally, chemical-based synthesis route suffers from compromised product selectivity, environmental pollution, and toxic impurities [ 7 ]. The rapid advance in synthetic biology and metabolic engineering offers an alternative strategy for the sustainable synthesis of high-value natural products [ 8 ]. Microbial production of limonene and its derivatives, such as perillyl alcohol, perillic acid and (+)-carveol, have been documented in Escherichia coli [ 9 ], Candida tropicalis [ 6 ], Saccharomyces cerevisiae [ 1 , 10 ], Yarrowia lipolytica [ 11 ], and Rhodotorula toruloides [ 7 ]. However, the de novo microbial production of (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone has been rarely reported ( Table 1 , Table 2 , Table 3 ).

Open in a new tab For facilitating monoterpenoids microbial production, the commonly employed strategies include: (i) screening natural enzymes with desired efficiency [ 6 , 17 ]; (ii) engineering enzymes through rational design or directed evolution [ 18 ]; (iii) fusing sequential and determinant enzymes to avoid metabolite flux leakage and accelerate substrate transformation [ 19 ]; (iv) optimizing the key knots in the biosynthesis pathway while down-tuning the competitive route to streamline precursor and intermediates supply toward downstream conversion [ 6 ]; (v) engineering the redox balance by recycling the essential cofactors like NAD(P)H [ 8 ]. Besides the integrated use of the metabolic engineering approaches, an appropriate microbial host can also contribute to the establishment of a monoterpenoid cell factory.
Although it currently has a less advanced genetic editing toolbox, the red yeast Rhodotorula toruloides is exhibiting attractive properties as a promising microbial cell factory for terpenoid production with the fast development of synthetic biology and metabolic engineering technology. Importantly, it harbors rich pool of acetyl-CoA and NADPH, broad substrate spectrum and outstanding high-density fermentation capacity. Besides, it has stronger robustness than other oleaginous yeasts such as Y. lipolytica in harsh conditions, which offers the advantage of refining low-cost feedstocks, such as non-detoxified hydrolysates of agricultural lignocellulosic biomass, toward value-added products [ [20] , [21] , [22] ]. Notably, it exhibits high tolerance to up to 2.0 g/L limonene, making it promising for limonene and derivatives production [ 22 ]. Additionally, it has been successfully engineered to produce a wide range of valuable compounds such as linalool, lipids and carotenoids [ [23] , [24] , [25] ]. Taken together, the natural attributes mentioned above position R. toruloides as a highly interesting chassis fo

### 2.1. Strains and culture conditions
Plasmid construction and propagation were conducted with E. coli DH5α in Luria−Bertani (LB) medium, supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin at 37 °C. LB medium was also used for cultivation of Agrobacterium tumefaciens AGL1 at 28 °C. The haploid R. toruloides NP11 was donated by Prof. Zongbao Zhao. If not specified, the yeast strains were cultured in nitrogen-limiting (NL) medium that were kept at 22 °C and 180 rpm for a time range as needed. Antibiotics (G418, nourseothricin, or zeocin, 50 μg/mL) were used for identifying yeast transformants in both liquid and solid YPD media (20 g/L agar was added into liquid YPD).

### 2.2. Plasmid construction
The vector pZPK was employed to construct all the necessary expression cassettes in this study [ 27 ]. The plasmids and primers used in this study are provided in supplementary materials. The DNA Ligation Kit Ver.2.1 (Takara) and In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara) were employed for constructing the vectors. All the genes used in this study were optimized according to the codon bias of R. toruloides and synthesized by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, P. R. China). The codon usage of the heterologous genes was redressed according to the preference of R. toruloides and produced by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, China). The heterologous (−)-LS genes were Cs tLS from Cannabis sativa ( NP_001384867.1 ), Et tLS from Eleutherococcus trifoliatus ( AIO10970.1 ), Ml tLS from Mentha longifolia ( WAB06559.1 ), Ms tLS from Mentha spicata ( QBA83293.1 ), Pa tLS from Pinus armandii Franch ( UNY86182.1 ), and Ps tLS from Picea abies ( AAS47694.1 ). The carvone dehydrogenase genes were Ab CDH from Actinobacteria bacterium (MGW3291715.1), Mp CDH from Mentha × piperita ( QPI35669.1 ), Re CDH from Rhodococcus erythropolis ( WP_076949156.1 ), Sh CDH from Streptomyces himastatinicus ( WP_009719709.1 ), Mt CDH from Mycolicibacterium thermoresistibile ( WP_448509721.1 ) and M y s CDH from Mycobacterium sp (HYJ57287.1). The acetoacetyl-CoA synthase NphT7, ( D7URV0 .1), Acetyl-CoA acetyl-transferase/HMGR ( Ef MvaE, AF290092 ), HMG-CoA synthase ( Ef MvaS, AF290092 ), Mevalonate kinase ( Mm MK, AAM31458 ). The native ATP-citrate lyase (ACL, RHTO_03915) was cloned from the cDNA of R . toruloides NP11. 2.3. Construction of recombinant R. toruloides

### 2.4. Fermentation of engineered strains
For flask fermentation, colonies were pre-cultured in 50-mL test tubes, containing 5 mL of YPD medium, at 28 °C, 180 rpm until OD 600 reached 10–12. Then, they were inoculated at an initial OD 600 of 0.5 in the 250-mL shake flasks (containing 50 mL NL, YPD or MM medium) and cultivated at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The carbon source used for production was 20 g/L glucose. Isopropyl myristate (IPM) was used as an overlay 20% (v/v) for the instant extraction of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone.

### 3.1. Construction of the (−)-limonene biosynthesis baseline
Limonene can be synthesized through the MVA and/or MEP pathway with geranyl diphosphate (GPP) and/or NPP as the direct precursor [ 19 ]. The biosynthesis of limonene is controlled by several rate-limiting enzyme, such as HMGR, IDI, GPP and/or NPP synthase and limonene synthase (LS) [ 6 , 7 ]. Moreover, fermentation conditions influence the cell viability and the final chemical productivity. Particularly, the carbon flux will be mostly directed towards lipid biosynthesis in R . toruloides under nutrient depleted conditions, such as nitrogen limitation [ 30 ]. Fortunately, we have previously constructed a MVA, NPP and fusion protein based limonene biosynthesis route, developed a mutant FPPS from R. toruloides (FPPS F91W/N122W/K192G , hereafter denoted as FPPS∗∗∗) to boost the efficient linalool synthesis in R. toruloides and isolated a strong promoter pLDP in NL medium [ 22 ].
Considering that the catalytic efficiency of the (−)-limonene synthase ((−)-LS) is crucial for high-yield biosynthesis, we first employed the most reported (−)-LS from Mentha spicata ( Ms tLS) to construct the (−)-limonene synthesis pathway [ 8 , 10 ]. It was fused to the FPPS∗∗∗ (FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS) with the GGGS linker, the most commonly used strategy to enhance the precuror transfer and limonene production [ 8 ]. To ensure the precursor supply, the critical enzymes HMGR was linked with FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS by P2A peptide and overexpressed simultaneously using the strong promoter pLDP1 ( Fig. 2 ). Then, five other distinct (−)-LSs (Phylogenetic analysis, Fig. S2A ) were fused to FPPS∗∗∗ with GGGS linker and compared for their capacity in supporting (−)-limonene production. The results showed that Ms tLS was the most effective among all the candidates ( Fig. 2 A). To further verify our results, we investigated the limonene production with the fusion protein ( Ms tLS-FPPS∗∗∗), and separate expression of Ms tLS and FPPS∗∗∗ mediated by P2A peptide. We also managed to constructed the nerol pyrophosphate (N

### 3.2. Strengthening the upper pathway and NADPH supply leads to enhanced (−)-limonene production
Optimizing the design of metabolic pathways is paramount for achieving efficient microbial synthesis of desired products. The MVA-based limonene synthesis pathway is initiated with the acetoacetyl-CoA, which is produced from condensing acetyl-CoA by gate-keeper enzyme ACCT, or acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA by the acac-CoA synthase (NphT7) from Streptomyces sp. ( Fig. 1 , Fig. 3 A) [ 31 , 32 ].
Biosynthetic pathway for (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone. Black, endogenous genes and pathways; Orange, introduced genes and pathways; Green, endogenous genes overexpressed. ### 3.3. (−)-Carveol biosynthesis from (−)-limonene
(−)-Carveol is a naturally oxygenated derivative of limonene, catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 enzyme (L6H) [ 44 , 45 ]. In addition, the L6H requires a cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR) to maintain its proper catalysis activity [ 46 ]. To convert (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, we recruited the Mentha x gracilis originated L6H ( Mg L6H) and the CPR from Arabidopsis thaliana ( At CPR) by putting them under the native pLDP1 ( Fig. 4 ), which have been demonstrated efficiency for limonene derivatives. Considering that the plant-derived P450s exhibit significant challenges for heterologous expression, including low catalytic efficiency and frequent substrate promiscuity [ 47 ], we strategically avoided using the strain SL12 with the highest (−)-limonene titer as the chassis cell. Instead, the medium strain SL4 that produced 51.0 mg/L (−)-limonene was chosen to circumvent excessive precursor accumulation.
Engineering the (−)-carveol biosynthesis. (A) The retention of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol on the gas chromatogram. The (−)-carveol standard mixtures were composed of (−)-cis-carveol and (−)-trans-carveol with a ratio of 11: 9. (B) The mass spectrum of (−)-carveol standard and the sample. (C) and (D) Optimization of the (−)-carveol synthesis by reinforcement the expression of critical genes in catalyzing carveol production and the MVA pathway. ns, no significant difference, ∗, p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗, p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.001; ∗∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.0001 (two-tailed unpaired Student's t -test). The experiments were conducted in triplicate and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. As expected, when the Mg L6H and At CPR were co-integrated into the genome of SL4, the resultant strain SC1 produced 22.9 mg/L (−)-carveol at an 80.6% ratio, with 5.2 mg/L (−)-limonene left ( Fig. 4 C) in NL medium at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The accumulation of (−)-limonene indicated that the (−)-carveol synthesis enzyme activity was less efficient and required further optimizati

### 3.4. Engineering the (−)-carvone biosynthesis
(−)-Carvone is converted from (−)-carveol via the carveol dehydrogenase (CDH) [ 50 ]. To construct the whole (−)-carvone biosynthesis pathway, six CDHs from distinct sources were evaluated with the (−)-carveol producing strain SC9. Phylogenetic analysis revealed evolutionary divergence among these enzymes, which might help the finding of CDH with desired activity ( Fig. S2B ). The (−)-carvone production suggested that the most efficient one was from R. erythropolis ( Re CDH) , which generated 5 mg/L (−)-carvone in 50-mL test tube ( Fig. 5 B). However, there were still a lot of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol left, which might be attributed to the undesired enzymatic activity ( Fig. 5 C). We thus hypothesized that the common metabolic engineering practice, increasing the gene copy numbers of the critical CDH would enhance the (−)-carvone production. As expected, the (−)-carvone was improved to 30 mg/L when the four copies of CDH were introduced into R. toruloides ( Fig. 5 D). While a sharp reduction in (−)-carveol accumulation was observed, a comparable amount of (−)-limonene was still produced ( Fig. 5 D). Moreover, our results also showed that the composition of the monoterpenoids were also strain-dependent as the sub-clones of the strain SE4 affected different monoterpenoids spectra ( Fig. 5 E). Furthermore, the (–)-carveol contents varied among tested subclones while the residue limonene remained almost comparable, suggesting that the conversion efficiency of limonene to carveol should be given more consideration. To ensure the satisfactory production of (−)-carvone, highly efficient L6H and CDH should be further explored.

### 3.5. Increase monoterpenoids production by fed-batch fermentation
We further increased (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production by fed-batch fermentation using SL14, SC9 and SE4, respectively. Prior to fed-batch fermentation, the influence of C/N ratios (15:1, 30:1, 60:1, 120:1, and 240:1) on (−)-limonene production was evaluated in 250-mL shake flask using SL9 since the availability of nutrients critically influences microbial growth and metabolic activity ( Fig. S3 ). Comparable (−)-limonene production was obtained when the C/N ratios were 15:1, 30:1 and 60:1 while severe impaired cell growth was observed with the C/N ratios of 120:1 and 240:1. The fed-batch fermentation results on 500-mL bioreactors demonstrated that the C/N ratio of 15:1 outperformed 30:1 and 60:1 since the highest (−)-limonene titer of 608.5 mg/L was achieved with a C/N ratio of 15:1 at 156 h ( Fig. S4 ). Subsequently, we scaled up the fermentation system to a 3-L bioreactor with a C/N ratio of 15:1 ( Fig. 6 A), which commenced the (−)-limonene production at 48 h, and maximized with a final production of 1.6 g/L and 19.0 mg/g glucose at 144 h.
Fed-batch fermentation of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol. (A) SL14 for (−)-limonene production and (B) SC9 for (−)-carveol production in 3-L bioreactors. The experiments were conducted in triplicate, and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. The C/N ratio of 15:1 was also applied to conduct the fed-batch fermentation of (−)-carveol with strain SC9 in the 3-L bioreactor, where the final (−)-carveol titer reached 668.0 mg/L at 240 h. However, a very high residue of (−)-limonene (361.7 mg/L) was also observed, 36% of the total monoterpenoids production ( Fig. 6 B). The significant accumulation of limonene suggested the hydroxylation of (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, determined by L6H and CPR, was a bottleneck for efficient (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production. The apparent increase in (−)-limonene accumulation in the bioreactors indicated the L6H catalytic efficiency was severely compromised,

### Abstract
De novo biosynthesis of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone was achieved via rewiring the mevalonate pathway in the oleaginous yeast Rhodotorula toruloides . Strategies including enzyme selection, protein fusion, pathway optimization (MVA upstream enhancement, cofactor supply), and fermentation condition optimization were applied to improve the monoterpenoids production. Finally, the (−)-limonene titer of 1.6 g/L and (−)-carveol of 668.0 mg/L were achieved through fed-batch fermentation in a 3-L bioreactor. Furthermore, the feasibility of biosynthesis of (−)-carvone was also demonstrated. This study represents an example for de novo microbial production of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone with the oleaginous red yeast R. toruloides , demonstrating its potential as a versatile chassis for monoterpenoid biosynthesis.

### 1. Introduction
Isoprene-derived monoterpenes find broad applications in food, pharmaceuticals, fragrances [ 1 , 2 ]. Among all the monoterpenes, (+)-limonene and (−)-limonene are enantiomers that possess distinct aromatic attributes [ 3 ]. While (+)-limonene is directly used as flavors, solvents and industrial feedstocks, (−)-limonene serves as precursors for valuable oxygenated monoterpenoids, such as (−)-menthol and perillic acid, which exhibits more desirable fragrance properties, significant economic and pharmacological values [ [4] , [5] , [6] ].
The traditional production of limonene and its oxygenated derivatives from plant sources usually faces uncertainties caused by climate variability, environmental changes, and cultivation area constraints. Additionally, chemical-based synthesis route suffers from compromised product selectivity, environmental pollution, and toxic impurities [ 7 ]. The rapid advance in synthetic biology and metabolic engineering offers an alternative strategy for the sustainable synthesis of high-value natural products [ 8 ]. Microbial production of limonene and its derivatives, such as perillyl alcohol, perillic acid and (+)-carveol, have been documented in Escherichia coli [ 9 ], Candida tropicalis [ 6 ], Saccharomyces cerevisiae [ 1 , 10 ], Yarrowia lipolytica [ 11 ], and Rhodotorula toruloides [ 7 ]. However, the de novo microbial production of (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone has been rarely reported ( Table 1 , Table 2 , Table 3 ).

### Table 1.

### Table 3.

Open in a new tab For facilitating monoterpenoids microbial production, the commonly employed strategies include: (i) screening natural enzymes with desired efficiency [ 6 , 17 ]; (ii) engineering enzymes through rational design or directed evolution [ 18 ]; (iii) fusing sequential and determinant enzymes to avoid metabolite flux leakage and accelerate substrate transformation [ 19 ]; (iv) optimizing the key knots in the biosynthesis pathway while down-tuning the competitive route to streamline precursor and intermediates supply toward downstream conversion [ 6 ]; (v) engineering the redox balance by recycling the essential cofactors like NAD(P)H [ 8 ]. Besides the integrated use of the metabolic engineering approaches, an appropriate microbial host can also contribute to the establishment of a monoterpenoid cell factory.
Although it currently has a less advanced genetic editing toolbox, the red yeast Rhodotorula toruloides is exhibiting attractive properties as a promising microbial cell factory for terpenoid production with the fast development of synthetic biology and metabolic engineering technology. Importantly, it harbors rich pool of acetyl-CoA and NADPH, broad substrate spectrum and outstanding high-density fermentation capacity. Besides, it has stronger robustness than other oleaginous yeasts such as Y. lipolytica in harsh conditions, which offers the advantage of refining low-cost feedstocks, such as non-detoxified hydrolysates of agricultural lignocellulosic biomass, toward value-added products [ [20] , [21] , [22] ]. Notably, it exhibits high tolerance to up to 2.0 g/L limonene, making it promising for limonene and derivatives production [ 22 ]. Additionally, it has been successfully engineered to produce a wide range of valuable compounds such as linalool, lipids and carotenoids [ [23] , [24] , [25] ]. Taken together, the natural attributes mentioned above position R. toruloides as a highly interesting chassis fo

### 2.1. Strains and culture conditions
Plasmid construction and propagation were conducted with E. coli DH5α in Luria−Bertani (LB) medium, supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin at 37 °C. LB medium was also used for cultivation of Agrobacterium tumefaciens AGL1 at 28 °C. The haploid R. toruloides NP11 was donated by Prof. Zongbao Zhao. If not specified, the yeast strains were cultured in nitrogen-limiting (NL) medium that were kept at 22 °C and 180 rpm for a time range as needed. Antibiotics (G418, nourseothricin, or zeocin, 50 μg/mL) were used for identifying yeast transformants in both liquid and solid YPD media (20 g/L agar was added into liquid YPD).

### 2.2. Plasmid construction
The vector pZPK was employed to construct all the necessary expression cassettes in this study [ 27 ]. The plasmids and primers used in this study are provided in supplementary materials. The DNA Ligation Kit Ver.2.1 (Takara) and In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara) were employed for constructing the vectors. All the genes used in this study were optimized according to the codon bias of R. toruloides and synthesized by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, P. R. China). The codon usage of the heterologous genes was redressed according to the preference of R. toruloides and produced by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, China). The heterologous (−)-LS genes were Cs tLS from Cannabis sativa ( NP_001384867.1 ), Et tLS from Eleutherococcus trifoliatus ( AIO10970.1 ), Ml tLS from Mentha longifolia ( WAB06559.1 ), Ms tLS from Mentha spicata ( QBA83293.1 ), Pa tLS from Pinus armandii Franch ( UNY86182.1 ), and Ps tLS from Picea abies ( AAS47694.1 ). The carvone dehydrogenase genes were Ab CDH from Actinobacteria bacterium (MGW3291715.1), Mp CDH from Mentha × piperita ( QPI35669.1 ), Re CDH from Rhodococcus erythropolis ( WP_076949156.1 ), Sh CDH from Streptomyces himastatinicus ( WP_009719709.1 ), Mt CDH from Mycolicibacterium thermoresistibile ( WP_448509721.1 ) and M y s CDH from Mycobacterium sp (HYJ57287.1). The acetoacetyl-CoA synthase NphT7, ( D7URV0 .1), Acetyl-CoA acetyl-transferase/HMGR ( Ef MvaE, AF290092 ), HMG-CoA synthase ( Ef MvaS, AF290092 ), Mevalonate kinase ( Mm MK, AAM31458 ). The native ATP-citrate lyase (ACL, RHTO_03915) was cloned from the cDNA of R . toruloides NP11. 2.3. Construction of recombinant R. toruloides

### 2.4. Fermentation of engineered strains
For flask fermentation, colonies were pre-cultured in 50-mL test tubes, containing 5 mL of YPD medium, at 28 °C, 180 rpm until OD 600 reached 10–12. Then, they were inoculated at an initial OD 600 of 0.5 in the 250-mL shake flasks (containing 50 mL NL, YPD or MM medium) and cultivated at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The carbon source used for production was 20 g/L glucose. Isopropyl myristate (IPM) was used as an overlay 20% (v/v) for the instant extraction of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone.

### 3.1. Construction of the (−)-limonene biosynthesis baseline
Limonene can be synthesized through the MVA and/or MEP pathway with geranyl diphosphate (GPP) and/or NPP as the direct precursor [ 19 ]. The biosynthesis of limonene is controlled by several rate-limiting enzyme, such as HMGR, IDI, GPP and/or NPP synthase and limonene synthase (LS) [ 6 , 7 ]. Moreover, fermentation conditions influence the cell viability and the final chemical productivity. Particularly, the carbon flux will be mostly directed towards lipid biosynthesis in R . toruloides under nutrient depleted conditions, such as nitrogen limitation [ 30 ]. Fortunately, we have previously constructed a MVA, NPP and fusion protein based limonene biosynthesis route, developed a mutant FPPS from R. toruloides (FPPS F91W/N122W/K192G , hereafter denoted as FPPS∗∗∗) to boost the efficient linalool synthesis in R. toruloides and isolated a strong promoter pLDP in NL medium [ 22 ].
Considering that the catalytic efficiency of the (−)-limonene synthase ((−)-LS) is crucial for high-yield biosynthesis, we first employed the most reported (−)-LS from Mentha spicata ( Ms tLS) to construct the (−)-limonene synthesis pathway [ 8 , 10 ]. It was fused to the FPPS∗∗∗ (FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS) with the GGGS linker, the most commonly used strategy to enhance the precuror transfer and limonene production [ 8 ]. To ensure the precursor supply, the critical enzymes HMGR was linked with FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS by P2A peptide and overexpressed simultaneously using the strong promoter pLDP1 ( Fig. 2 ). Then, five other distinct (−)-LSs (Phylogenetic analysis, Fig. S2A ) were fused to FPPS∗∗∗ with GGGS linker and compared for their capacity in supporting (−)-limonene production. The results showed that Ms tLS was the most effective among all the candidates ( Fig. 2 A). To further verify our results, we investigated the limonene production with the fusion protein ( Ms tLS-FPPS∗∗∗), and separate expression of Ms tLS and FPPS∗∗∗ mediated by P2A peptide. We also managed to constructed the nerol pyrophosphate (N

### 3.2. Strengthening the upper pathway and NADPH supply leads to enhanced (−)-limonene production
Optimizing the design of metabolic pathways is paramount for achieving efficient microbial synthesis of desired products. The MVA-based limonene synthesis pathway is initiated with the acetoacetyl-CoA, which is produced from condensing acetyl-CoA by gate-keeper enzyme ACCT, or acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA by the acac-CoA synthase (NphT7) from Streptomyces sp. ( Fig. 1 , Fig. 3 A) [ 31 , 32 ].

### 3.3. (−)-Carveol biosynthesis from (−)-limonene
(−)-Carveol is a naturally oxygenated derivative of limonene, catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 enzyme (L6H) [ 44 , 45 ]. In addition, the L6H requires a cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR) to maintain its proper catalysis activity [ 46 ]. To convert (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, we recruited the Mentha x gracilis originated L6H ( Mg L6H) and the CPR from Arabidopsis thaliana ( At CPR) by putting them under the native pLDP1 ( Fig. 4 ), which have been demonstrated efficiency for limonene derivatives. Considering that the plant-derived P450s exhibit significant challenges for heterologous expression, including low catalytic efficiency and frequent substrate promiscuity [ 47 ], we strategically avoided using the strain SL12 with the highest (−)-limonene titer as the chassis cell. Instead, the medium strain SL4 that produced 51.0 mg/L (−)-limonene was chosen to circumvent excessive precursor accumulation.
Engineering the (−)-carveol biosynthesis. (A) The retention of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol on the gas chromatogram. The (−)-carveol standard mixtures were composed of (−)-cis-carveol and (−)-trans-carveol with a ratio of 11: 9. (B) The mass spectrum of (−)-carveol standard and the sample. (C) and (D) Optimization of the (−)-carveol synthesis by reinforcement the expression of critical genes in catalyzing carveol production and the MVA pathway. ns, no significant difference, ∗, p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗, p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.001; ∗∗∗∗, p &lt; 0.0001 (two-tailed unpaired Student's t -test). The experiments were conducted in triplicate and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. As expected, when the Mg L6H and At CPR were co-integrated into the genome of SL4, the resultant strain SC1 produced 22.9 mg/L (−)-carveol at an 80.6% ratio, with 5.2 mg/L (−)-limonene left ( Fig. 4 C) in NL medium at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The accumulation of (−)-limonene indicated that the (−)-carveol synthesis enzyme activity was less efficient and required further optimizati

### 3.4. Engineering the (−)-carvone biosynthesis
(−)-Carvone is converted from (−)-carveol via the carveol dehydrogenase (CDH) [ 50 ]. To construct the whole (−)-carvone biosynthesis pathway, six CDHs from distinct sources were evaluated with the (−)-carveol producing strain SC9. Phylogenetic analysis revealed evolutionary divergence among these enzymes, which might help the finding of CDH with desired activity ( Fig. S2B ). The (−)-carvone production suggested that the most efficient one was from R. erythropolis ( Re CDH) , which generated 5 mg/L (−)-carvone in 50-mL test tube ( Fig. 5 B). However, there were still a lot of (−)-limonene and (−)-carveol left, which might be attributed to the undesired enzymatic activity ( Fig. 5 C). We thus hypothesized that the common metabolic engineering practice, increasing the gene copy numbers of the critical CDH would enhance the (−)-carvone production. As expected, the (−)-carvone was improved to 30 mg/L when the four copies of CDH were introduced into R. toruloides ( Fig. 5 D). While a sharp reduction in (−)-carveol accumulation was observed, a comparable amount of (−)-limonene was still produced ( Fig. 5 D). Moreover, our results also showed that the composition of the monoterpenoids were also strain-dependent as the sub-clones of the strain SE4 affected different monoterpenoids spectra ( Fig. 5 E). Furthermore, the (–)-carveol contents varied among tested subclones while the residue limonene remained almost comparable, suggesting that the conversion efficiency of limonene to carveol should be given more consideration. To ensure the satisfactory production of (−)-carvone, highly efficient L6H and CDH should be further explored.

### 3.5. Increase monoterpenoids production by fed-batch fermentation
We further increased (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production by fed-batch fermentation using SL14, SC9 and SE4, respectively. Prior to fed-batch fermentation, the influence of C/N ratios (15:1, 30:1, 60:1, 120:1, and 240:1) on (−)-limonene production was evaluated in 250-mL shake flask using SL9 since the availability of nutrients critically influences microbial growth and metabolic activity ( Fig. S3 ). Comparable (−)-limonene production was obtained when the C/N ratios were 15:1, 30:1 and 60:1 while severe impaired cell growth was observed with the C/N ratios of 120:1 and 240:1. The fed-batch fermentation results on 500-mL bioreactors demonstrated that the C/N ratio of 15:1 outperformed 30:1 and 60:1 since the highest (−)-limonene titer of 608.5 mg/L was achieved with a C/N ratio of 15:1 at 156 h ( Fig. S4 ). Subsequently, we scaled up the fermentation system to a 3-L bioreactor with a C/N ratio of 15:1 ( Fig. 6 A), which commenced the (−)-limonene production at 48 h, and maximized with a final production of 1.6 g/L and 19.0 mg/g glucose at 144 h.
Fed-batch fermentation of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol. (A) SL14 for (−)-limonene production and (B) SC9 for (−)-carveol production in 3-L bioreactors. The experiments were conducted in triplicate, and the results were presented as means and standard deviations. The C/N ratio of 15:1 was also applied to conduct the fed-batch fermentation of (−)-carveol with strain SC9 in the 3-L bioreactor, where the final (−)-carveol titer reached 668.0 mg/L at 240 h. However, a very high residue of (−)-limonene (361.7 mg/L) was also observed, 36% of the total monoterpenoids production ( Fig. 6 B). The significant accumulation of limonene suggested the hydroxylation of (−)-limonene to (−)-carveol, determined by L6H and CPR, was a bottleneck for efficient (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone production. ### Abstract
De novo biosynthesis of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone was achieved via rewiring the mevalonate pathway in the oleaginous yeast Rhodotorula toruloides . Strategies including enzyme selection, protein fusion, pathway optimization (MVA upstream enhancement, cofactor supply), and fermentation condition optimization were applied to improve the monoterpenoids production. Finally, the (−)-limonene titer of 1.6 g/L and (−)-carveol of 668.0 mg/L were achieved through fed-batch fermentation in a 3-L bioreactor. Furthermore, the feasibility of biosynthesis of (−)-carvone was also demonstrated. This study represents an example for de novo microbial production of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone with the oleaginous red yeast R. toruloides , demonstrating its potential as a versatile chassis for monoterpenoid biosynthesis.

### 1. Introduction
Isoprene-derived monoterpenes find broad applications in food, pharmaceuticals, fragrances [ 1 , 2 ]. Among all the monoterpenes, (+)-limonene and (−)-limonene are enantiomers that possess distinct aromatic attributes [ 3 ]. While (+)-limonene is directly used as flavors, solvents and industrial feedstocks, (−)-limonene serves as precursors for valuable oxygenated monoterpenoids, such as (−)-menthol and perillic acid, which exhibits more desirable fragrance properties, significant economic and pharmacological values [ [4] , [5] , [6] ].
The traditional production of limonene and its oxygenated derivatives from plant sources usually faces uncertainties caused by climate variability, environmental changes, and cultivation area constraints. Additionally, chemical-based synthesis route suffers from compromised product selectivity, environmental pollution, and toxic impurities [ 7 ]. The rapid advance in synthetic biology and metabolic engineering offers an alternative strategy for the sustainable synthesis of high-value natural products [ 8 ]. Microbial production of limonene and its derivatives, such as perillyl alcohol, perillic acid and (+)-carveol, have been documented in Escherichia coli [ 9 ], Candida tropicalis [ 6 ], Saccharomyces cerevisiae [ 1 , 10 ], Yarrowia lipolytica [ 11 ], and Rhodotorula toruloides [ 7 ]. However, the de novo microbial production of (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone has been rarely reported ( Table 1 , Table 2 , Table 3 ).

Open in a new tab For facilitating monoterpenoids microbial production, the commonly employed strategies include: (i) screening natural enzymes with desired efficiency [ 6 , 17 ]; (ii) engineering enzymes through rational design or directed evolution [ 18 ]; (iii) fusing sequential and determinant enzymes to avoid metabolite flux leakage and accelerate substrate transformation [ 19 ]; (iv) optimizing the key knots in the biosynthesis pathway while down-tuning the competitive route to streamline precursor and intermediates supply toward downstream conversion [ 6 ]; (v) engineering the redox balance by recycling the essential cofactors like NAD(P)H [ 8 ]. Besides the integrated use of the metabolic engineering approaches, an appropriate microbial host can also contribute to the establishment of a monoterpenoid cell factory.
Although it currently has a less advanced genetic editing toolbox, the red yeast Rhodotorula toruloides is exhibiting attractive properties as a promising microbial cell factory for terpenoid production with the fast development of synthetic biology and metabolic engineering technology. Importantly, it harbors rich pool of acetyl-CoA and NADPH, broad substrate spectrum and outstanding high-density fermentation capacity. Besides, it has stronger robustness than other oleaginous yeasts such as Y. lipolytica in harsh conditions, which offers the advantage of refining low-cost feedstocks, such as non-detoxified hydrolysates of agricultural lignocellulosic biomass, toward value-added products [ [20] , [21] , [22] ]. Notably, it exhibits high tolerance to up to 2.0 g/L limonene, making it promising for limonene and derivatives production [ 22 ]. Additionally, it has been successfully engineered to produce a wide range of valuable compounds such as linalool, lipids and carotenoids [ [23] , [24] , [25] ]. Taken together, the natural attributes mentioned above position R. toruloides as a highly interesting chassis fo

### 2.1. Strains and culture conditions
Plasmid construction and propagation were conducted with E. coli DH5α in Luria−Bertani (LB) medium, supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin at 37 °C. LB medium was also used for cultivation of Agrobacterium tumefaciens AGL1 at 28 °C. The haploid R. toruloides NP11 was donated by Prof. Zongbao Zhao. If not specified, the yeast strains were cultured in nitrogen-limiting (NL) medium that were kept at 22 °C and 180 rpm for a time range as needed. Antibiotics (G418, nourseothricin, or zeocin, 50 μg/mL) were used for identifying yeast transformants in both liquid and solid YPD media (20 g/L agar was added into liquid YPD).

### 2.2. Plasmid construction
The vector pZPK was employed to construct all the necessary expression cassettes in this study [ 27 ]. The plasmids and primers used in this study are provided in supplementary materials. The DNA Ligation Kit Ver.2.1 (Takara) and In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara) were employed for constructing the vectors. All the genes used in this study were optimized according to the codon bias of R. toruloides and synthesized by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, P. R. China). The codon usage of the heterologous genes was redressed according to the preference of R. toruloides and produced by Synbio Technologies (Suzhou, China). The heterologous (−)-LS genes were Cs tLS from Cannabis sativa ( NP_001384867.1 ), Et tLS from Eleutherococcus trifoliatus ( AIO10970.1 ), Ml tLS from Mentha longifolia ( WAB06559.1 ), Ms tLS from Mentha spicata ( QBA83293.1 ), Pa tLS from Pinus armandii Franch ( UNY86182.1 ), and Ps tLS from Picea abies ( AAS47694.1 ). The carvone dehydrogenase genes were Ab CDH from Actinobacteria bacterium (MGW3291715.1), Mp CDH from Mentha × piperita ( QPI35669.1 ), Re CDH from Rhodococcus erythropolis ( WP_076949156.1 ), Sh CDH from Streptomyces himastatinicus ( WP_009719709.1 ), Mt CDH from Mycolicibacterium thermoresistibile ( WP_448509721.1 ) and M y s CDH from Mycobacterium sp (HYJ57287.1). The acetoacetyl-CoA synthase NphT7, ( D7URV0 .1), Acetyl-CoA acetyl-transferase/HMGR ( Ef MvaE, AF290092 ), HMG-CoA synthase ( Ef MvaS, AF290092 ), Mevalonate kinase ( Mm MK, AAM31458 ). The native ATP-citrate lyase (ACL, RHTO_03915) was cloned from the cDNA of R . toruloides NP11. 2.3. Construction of recombinant R. toruloides

### 2.4. Fermentation of engineered strains
For flask fermentation, colonies were pre-cultured in 50-mL test tubes, containing 5 mL of YPD medium, at 28 °C, 180 rpm until OD 600 reached 10–12. Then, they were inoculated at an initial OD 600 of 0.5 in the 250-mL shake flasks (containing 50 mL NL, YPD or MM medium) and cultivated at 22 °C and 180 rpm for 120 h. The carbon source used for production was 20 g/L glucose. Isopropyl myristate (IPM) was used as an overlay 20% (v/v) for the instant extraction of (−)-limonene, (−)-carveol and (−)-carvone.

### 3.1. Construction of the (−)-limonene biosynthesis baseline
Limonene can be synthesized through the MVA and/or MEP pathway with geranyl diphosphate (GPP) and/or NPP as the direct precursor [ 19 ]. The biosynthesis of limonene is controlled by several rate-limiting enzyme, such as HMGR, IDI, GPP and/or NPP synthase and limonene synthase (LS) [ 6 , 7 ]. Moreover, fermentation conditions influence the cell viability and the final chemical productivity. Particularly, the carbon flux will be mostly directed towards lipid biosynthesis in R . toruloides under nutrient depleted conditions, such as nitrogen limitation [ 30 ]. Fortunately, we have previously constructed a MVA, NPP and fusion protein based limonene biosynthesis route, developed a mutant FPPS from R. toruloides (FPPS F91W/N122W/K192G , hereafter denoted as FPPS∗∗∗) to boost the efficient linalool synthesis in R. toruloides and isolated a strong promoter pLDP in NL medium [ 22 ].
Considering that the catalytic efficiency of the (−)-limonene synthase ((−)-LS) is crucial for high-yield biosynthesis, we first employed the most reported (−)-LS from Mentha spicata ( Ms tLS) to construct the (−)-limonene synthesis pathway [ 8 , 10 ]. It was fused to the FPPS∗∗∗ (FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS) with the GGGS linker, the most commonly used strategy to enhance the precuror transfer and limonene production [ 8 ]. To ensure the precursor supply, the critical enzymes HMGR was linked with FPPS∗∗∗- Ms tLS by P2A peptide and overexpressed simultaneously using the strong promoter pLDP1 ( Fig. 2 ). Then, five other distinct (−)-LSs (Phylogenetic analysis, Fig. S2A ) were fused to FPPS∗∗∗ with GGGS linker and compared for their capacity in supporting (−)-limonene production. The results showed that Ms tLS was the most effective among all the candidates ( Fig. 2 A). To further verify our results, we investigated the limonene production with the fusion protein ( Ms tLS-FPPS∗∗∗), and separate expression of Ms tLS and FPPS∗∗∗ mediated by P2A peptide. We also managed to constructed the nerol pyrophosphate (N

### 3.2. Strengthening the upper pathway and NADPH supply leads to enhanced (−)-limonene production
Optimizing the design of metabolic pathways is paramount for achieving efficient microbial synthesis of desired products. The MVA-based limonene synthesis pathway is initiated with the acetoacetyl-CoA, which is produced from condensing acetyl-CoA by gate-keeper enzyme ACCT, or acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA by the acac-CoA synthase (NphT7) from Streptomyces sp. ( Fig. 1 , Fig. 3 A) [ 31 , 32 ].
